fields.country: Egypt; India; China (fieldwork also in the United Kingdom archives and the United States)
fields.subnational_unit: Cairo, Mumbai and Shanghai (megacities with 40-60% of residents in informal settlements)
fields.population: stigmatised street-working and informal-settlement populations (fruit vendors in Cairo, hijras in Mumbai), state and municipal sanitation officials, and teams developing "reinvented toilets"
fields.sample_size: multi-sited fieldwork: Egypt summer 2019, India spring and autumn 2022, China spring 2023; archival documents 1850-1950 (London); interviews (number not stated), participant observation, digital ethnography, discourse analysis of media and government texts, toilet mapping, Gates Foundation Reinvent the Toilet documents and grantee interviews
fields.effect_measure: interdisciplinary qualitative analysis (archival, ethnographic, discourse analysis, toilet mapping); no quantitative measure
fields.effect_estimate: Argues that national "sanitation for all" campaigns in Egypt, India and China are sites of biopolitical and bioeconomic state regulation: they extend state control over bodies and public space, criminalise poverty and street work, use enforcement and surveillance measures (facial-recognition cameras, social-media shaming campaigns, toilets that analyse excreta) and treat human waste as a source of capital and biodata, rather than simply providing public works. Offers a colonial-period history of sanitation regulation (military cantonment sex-work regulation). No effect estimate.
fields.model_type: interdisciplinary qualitative case-study analysis (archival, ethnographic, discourse analysis)
fields.study_design: comparative qualitative multi-sited ethnographic and archival dissertation of three megacities

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a comparative qualitative dissertation (archival, ethnographic and discourse analysis; Cairo, Mumbai, Shanghai) on sanitation mega-projects as state regulation and surveillance, read in full text 2026-10-04 (abstract, introduction and methods; chapters only partly read). Enforcement and criminalisation of poverty are central themes; no effect estimate, and its link to household access conditions is indirect.
